frame.text: A shift at a desk in 2016, editing other women's testimony for an organisation that says it is helping them. The day ends because other people, somewhere else, stop doing the same work.

close._doc: What the era leaves behind, for the Close to read.

body: Era 3 dramatises a shift of ordinary content work inside an organisation that runs conversion practices: editing testimony, moderating replies, answering families, cutting promotional media and pricing a course. The organisations, the platform, the assistant, the course, the group and every person in the era are INVENTED. The practices they perform are drawn from a documented record, and the cards below say for each claim how well documented it is.

⚑ One fact in the era is real and is not ours: Malta's Affirmation of Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act — Act LV of 2016 — was passed unanimously and made Malta the first country in Europe to ban conversion practices. The newspaper reporting it in the piece is invented. The law is not.

⚑ And one thing the record does NOT show is itself a finding, stated here rather than papered over: there is little published evidence of the ordinary message traffic of private ex-lesbian accountability groups around 2016. The group in this era is written into that gap openly — invented name, invented members, invented sentences, documented shape.

sources.text: Peer accountability groups are a real instrument of ex-gay ministry, not an invented device. In programmes such as Living Waters, membership is closed and justified by confidentiality, the group sits inside a structured course, and it is facilitated — coordinators, small-group leaders, assistant leaders and pastoral overseers are named roles, and leaders are trained. The group in the piece has a facilitator for this reason and is not a leaderless circle.

Accountability covers far more than sexual acts. Programme material such as Living Waters' asks about family history, trauma, and relational and sexual concerns, and its teaching names emotional dependency and codependency; accountability software, adjacent to it, reports what a person looked at online. A member disclosing a hard night on which nothing happened is the documented shape, not a softening of it.

In the programme material, a reported lapse is framed as something to confess, pray through and keep working on — honesty, confession, forgiveness, healing prayer, boundaries. No rule was found that a lapse means removal (though breaking the group's confidentiality can). ⚑ No source was found for a formal escalation ladder (warning, sponsor call, removal), and the piece therefore contains none.

The women's strand of ex-gay ministry developed a vocabulary of its own, alongside the masculinised 'gender deficit' literature written for men: EMOTIONAL DEPENDENCY above all, alongside enmeshment, relational wounds, boundaries, unmet emotional need and a femininity to be recovered. Robinson and Spivey's peer-reviewed discourse analysis (Social Sciences 4(3), 2015) identifies 'emotional dependency' as a characteristic euphemism for female homosexuality. Every line of the era's course, group and podcast copy is written from this register.

Movement material repeatedly separates the person from the sexual identity — 'same-sex attracted', 'struggling with homosexuality', 'lesbian-identified', a person 'affected by' lesbianism — rather than accepting 'lesbian' as a stable category. ⚑ The first correction the player is asked to apply in the era replaces 'lesbian' with 'same-sex attracted'. That beat was written before this research and turns out to be the documented move.

Father and mother 'wounds', disrupted gender development and relational brokenness are taught by some of these ministries as causal or formative explanations for same-sex attraction. ⚑ THESE ETIOLOGICAL CLAIMS ARE NOT ESTABLISHED PSYCHOLOGICAL SCIENCE. The piece renders them ONLY in the organisation's own voice — a course module, a correction's rationale — and nothing in the piece's own voice endorses them.
sources._statusS179: ⚑ S179 (Sérgio, 2026-09-27, 'yes to all four'): disputed → documented: it documents what some ministries taught, and says in the same breath that it is not established science (C6).

sources.text: By the middle of the period, evangelical sexual-accountability infrastructure had moved onto smartphones, transmitting browsing and activity reports to selected 'accountability partners' — advertised with unlimited partners, and turning episodic self-report into persistent observation another person could later question. ⚑ This is ADJACENT evidence from the purity-technology ecology, not proof that an ex-lesbian organisation used such a tool; the piece's assistant is invented and this material informs its affordances only.

Accountability products sold monitoring in the language of care: trust, support, help — automated behavioural reporting was marketed as a way to start a trusted conversation. ⚑ The piece takes that as Era 3's governing register: a person is asked how she is because somebody cares; hard questions are 'accountability'; scrutiny is help identifying temptation. Nothing in Era 3 is ever supposed to SOUND like surveillance.

Families are treated as a ministry of their own, with their own groups, appointments and curriculum — Harvest USA calls it its Parents & Family Ministry. Its parents' curriculum, Shattered Dreams, New Hope, gives grief a chapter of its own. Parents are told to keep the relationship without affirming the identity — to hold grace and truth together, to love without condoning, and to keep their own house's rules.
sources._r3S181: ⚑ S181 (Sérgio, 2026-09-27: 'approve round 3' — and 'make all text more explicit, instead of so defensive. We are not making this to justify, we are explaining what was used'): rewritten from docs/SOURCE_VERIFICATION_RESULTS_2026-09-27.md.

sources.text: An influential conservative source explicitly rejected advising parents to break off contact (the US Catholic bishops' Always Our Children, 1997), and the project's searches found no organisational document instructing families to withdraw support or to route an adult child's communications through the organisation. The era's family screen therefore contains no such template. The harm it dramatises is an indefinite holding pattern of patience and prayer that never answers the question a mother actually asked.

Family programmes are run as parallel support for families. No public document was found authorising a worker to report an enrolled adult's progress to a relative — nor one forbidding it. ⚑ The piece builds its family screen on that gap — the worker knows the mother's story because the mother told her, and the daughter has no record on the screen at all.

sources.confidence: low — testimony about providers, not providers' protocols
sources.text: Survivor and interview evidence, including a UK government-commissioned qualitative study, records people undergoing change efforts being advised to distance themselves from LGBT friends and discouraged from disclosing their sexuality, and losing faith-community support after accepting an LGBT identity. ⚑ These are reported experiences rather than written organisational policy, and the piece must not present them as the latter.
sources._statusS179: ⚑ S179 (Sérgio, 2026-09-27, 'yes to all four'): disputed → documented: a qualitative finding, stated as one (C12).

sources.text: Malta's Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Gender Expression Act (Act LV of 2016; introduced as the 'Affirmation of…' bill) was passed unanimously, making Malta the first country in Europe to prohibit conversion practices, with penalties for practitioners. ⚑ The masthead reporting it in the piece is INVENTED; the law is real and is never dramatised beyond what it did.

⚑ THE ERA'S ENDING IS OURS AND IS NOT A FINDING. That a coordinated refusal by enough participants can outrun an organisation's capacity to suppress it is the piece's argument, dramatised as a group sharing a link faster than a block can process it. No source claims this, the project lead has never claimed it as a finding, and the Dossier must carry the distinction for a reader who has not had that conversation.

sources.confidence: none — the record is thin and the fiction fills it openly
sources.text: ⚑ WHAT COULD NOT BE SOURCED, listed so the piece is not read as claiming it: that daily phone-group check-ins were a standard ex-lesbian form (a 2024 leader's guide for one general programme does recommend daily accountability by group text; that is not a historical standard); any terms of direct address between members; greeting formulas, emoji conventions, response-time or screenshot norms; a movement-wide word for a woman who leaves; and any particular messaging platform as a 2016 norm. The group's name, members and every sentence in it are invented. Its SHAPE is documented; its texture is ours.

sources._doc: ⚑ S195 — his 'B)' (2026-09-28): the recommendation gets a practice of its own, documented through this sentence (PLAN_WEB_AND_HELPERS §4). Grounding: his research SocialMedia_Deep.md §3 (GPAHE's audits of search and platform results); the report's link is verified in docs/SOURCE_VERIFICATION_RESULTS_2026-09-27.md. His wording wins.
sources.text: Recommendation follows vocabulary. GPAHE's audits of search and platform results (Conversion Therapy Online, 2023) found that the movement's own euphemisms — "unwanted same-sex attraction", "overcoming same-sex attraction" — surfaced conversion providers and sympathetic material, where the explicit term surfaced critical information; and that moderation was uneven by platform and above all by language. The organisations chose the words; the platforms did the routing. Era 3's tagging and Era 2's recommended thread are that shape.

sources._doc: ⚑ S201 — his approval (2026-09-29): 'Yes to all of them… this is important to not be minimized… As long as every element that makes these decisions is explained on the sources.' Verification: docs/reinterp/SOURCES_LIA_COLLECTION_2026-09-28.md §7.
sources.text: The 2003 ministry site is built on a documented one. Evergreen International's homepage (captured 28 October 2004) was organised by audience — Individuals, Family, Support Groups, Therapists and Church Leaders — with "The Way Out", a bookstore, events and an annual conference; its About page described a computer database of referrals, more than fifty affiliate support groups, printed information packets and conferences of about five hundred people. The piece's Harbor keeps that shape under an invented name, with forum software of the period.

sources._doc: ⚑ S205 — APPROVED by him as written (2026-10-01); S208: his yes (2026-10-02) to the two corrections in VERIFY_TESTIMONY_LINKS_2026-10-01.md (Truth in Love TV from 1999; I Do Exist as the evidence supports). Grounding: his research 'Yes — the testimony layer is historically…' (2026-10-01), mapped in docs/reinterp/SOURCES_TESTIMONY_2026-10-01.md; links held there until he has checked them.
sources.text: Testimony became media. Ex-gay ministries turned personal stories of change into repeatable objects: Love in Action's own history begins with its founder's "testimony and a newspaper ad"; Focus on the Family's Love Won Out conferences (from 1998) put former-gay speakers on stage as evidence; the "Truth in Love" campaign ran such stories from 1998 as newspaper advertisements and, from 1999, as television commercials ending in a contact number; and the 2004 documentary I Do Exist gathered five stories with expert framing and was sold on VHS and DVD as a discussion starter for churches, schools and universities. By 2008 its producer had disowned the film as evidence of change and was offering it only on limited terms; one of its participants later wrote publicly about leaving the movement. Era 2's Your Story is that life cycle: his record, his words, the ministry's story, its media object, and a doorway for somebody else.
